utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Glasnovic. Let us continue with the questions. I will begin with the following question: The Prosecution affirms that the HVO began, in April 1993, a systematic and a widespread cleansing, or rather, a campaign of persecution of Muslim civilians, with the goal of obtaining ethnically cleansed territories on which Croats live. What would you answer to such a claim, answer to Their Honours in that respect?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my observation, and on my experience in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1991 and until up to now, I would say that there is an error in this theory. It's a false -- it's false.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why? What is your knowledge in connection with that? That is what the Chamber would be interested in hearing. What is your knowledge concerning that, and why?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one thing, the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not one conflict; it was a series of conflicts that sometimes made renaissance Italy look like Disneyland. I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to add that the date is also an enigma to me, why that date is stated as start of the Muslim/Croat antagonism, because to my knowledge, the first conflict started at the local level, in the summer of 1992, in the municipality of Uskoplje. The next -- I can list all these chronologically if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next conflict that I'm aware of is a split in the Croat/Muslim alliance during the defence of Jajce. While reinforcements were rushed to Jajce in the fall of 1990, the beginning of October, to be exact, Muslim roadblocks -- and here I will use the terminology MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which means Muslim armed forces, and not the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because then it did not exist as such, and no attempt was made to integrate the Federation army until after the signing of the Dayton Agreement. So in the beginning of October 1992, MOS units blocked reinforcement routes to Jajce. The next conflict started in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me. We must explain to the Chamber who blocked the road and why were the Croatian forces coming to defend Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues] ... road was blocked. There was only one way into Jajce, and it was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And why? Also Muslims live in Jajce, don't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... make an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Deduct any assumptions or speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road was blocked. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have difficulties because of the previous translations is continued, so the answers and the questions mingle together. We cannot make a proper judgement from the transcript. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, the question itself asked the witness to speculate why these Muslims, why these MOS forces, as he called them, did this, which there is no basis to believe -- any reason to believe he knows or he can speculate as to why the Muslims did something. Secondly, again, the witness himself said, "I can only assume." I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No. Sorry, Your Honour. I'm not saying no to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think you have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I went through the questions and the translations of the transcript. I wasn't asking the assumptions, for the assumptions, but the knowledge, personal knowledge. I wanted to hear whether you personally went to Jajce with your units.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when I say "assume," I mean that I was not there directly at the time, but I know these things took place because at my headquarters we had a daily situation report and a daily briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please, so personal knowledge or the basis for the assertion. Please, your personal knowledge once again, and no assumptions, or if somebody -- a person with a name and surname stated something which would be the basis of your assertion.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... numerous officers, because I was interested in the start of the -- I say the early start of the polarisation, and I received concrete answers from the commander of the defence of Jajce, Mr. Simunovic, and also I believe General Pilipovic. I can continue. Excuse me. After the Prozor conflict, the fighting started in Uskoplje in January of 1993. I was personally involved in the Prozor conflict, and also the one in Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The first question: Who was the first to attack in all these incidents you've listed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, both on the basis of tu quoque and to relevance. It's nothing to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think at the beginning of this trial we also said that this Trial Chamber cannot accept the tu quoque defence, unless you show that this incident has something to do with what happened later here with the testimony of this witness. Otherwise we have some doubts as to the relevance of this evidence to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bear with me. I will begin thinking that I'm doing a futile job. Because in the indictment we have a clear statement and also with the evidence connected, that the HVO, from the month of April, began attacking and began carrying out ethnic cleansing of civilians. That is a crucial moment of this trial. We are presenting evidence that we did not begin attacking, that this all began a year earlier. But in order to arrive to the April -- to the 5th of May and June, and if the Chamber doesn't receive the evidence of this witness, who gave an oath, we will not be able to come to the truth of it. It's not the question of tu quoque, and we cannot, under the mantle of tu quoque, not to allow the Defence to -- not to attack the indictment in its key points. Mostar, on the 9th of May, or the 14th of April, it's not something that came out of the blue. We have a witness who has been in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to the present day, with the highest rank, and, as with other witnesses, he is under oath. That is for the sake of fairness, of justice, and the truth, to hear the truth. And then why is the Prosecutor, through his cross-examination, from Stolac and Prozor, carrying out cross-examination of witnesses? And here is a man and a witness who was in Prozor, and he will be able to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, first of all, I would like to say that this Trial Chamber is addressing the personal responsibility rather than the responsibility of an organisation like HVO. Secondly, I must say that the evidence you present must be related to the specific counts charged in the indictment. Thirdly, since you claim that the testimony of this witness will be related to the widespread and systematic attacks of the Muslims, we'll let you go for a while, to see how far you can reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in addition to that, here we have personal responsibility, and that the campaign was headed by my client, and it's connected with all the items in the indictment. So it is linked on the personal basis. Because you know perfectly well what the Prosecution said, President Tudjman ordered and then he quoted who was carried it out [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you were in Prozor. The Prosecution is saying that the houses were burned down, people were persecuted.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like to say first, is that the theory of ethnic cleansing, planned terror, to me is an enigma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this. First of all, there's no question pending about this. Number 2, this witness is not an expert. He's not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He has not come here as a political expert or an historian or a sociologist. I certainly have not objected to things that reasonable within his military, direct military experience. But since we started today, he has gone into a number of simply nothing more than personal opinion, matters on which has not been tendered or recognised by the Chamber as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you know, in the live testimony, we only want to hear what you saw and what you heard at that moment. So there's no speculation and assumption of any events. Just tell us what you saw and what you did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you as a commander, you, from 1992 onwards, did you receive an order or execute ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone lets me finish to the end, I will explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. It's not up to this witness to decide what's appropriate testimony. It's up to the Chamber to decide, and my objection stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear what the witness is going to tell us, whether his testimony is relevant to the issue or not.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I start to talk about the details in Prozor, I would like to say one thing. The basis for successful military campaign, a planned campaign, two things are needed: Mission, a clear mission; and clear intent. And, I, as a brigade commander, during the Prozor conflict, would have had to have known the intent of my commander, not just one level up, but two levels up. That means not only that zone headquarters, but also via HVO headquarters. No order, verbal or written, was given, nor any warning order, which precedes any operation, to do what you're suggesting was done in Prozor. I was in Prozor on the 22nd. I was there the day before the conflict started. I was there on a formal visit because my right wing was covered by the Rama Brigade. At the time, there were two headquarters in the city of Prozor, the town of Prozor. The formal TO, so-called, and the HVO. I spoke to both commanders and I saw no warning signals that a conflict was about to begin. The next day I received a communique from the chief of staff of the Rama Brigade, which I gave to this Tribunal my last visit here, saying that fighting had broken out in Prozor. He had learned this at a joint meeting between the two staffs, the TO and the HVO. During the course of the meeting, an HVO member, Franjo Zadro, was killed by a Muslim soldier. That is when the conflict escalated. I learned later that the TO had left the positions which they held together with the HVO against Republika Srpska, and I also -- I visited that line also in the previous week, and both components were still on the line. Weapons and equipment had started to disappear from stores, and the town, during my visit, was practically divided into upper and lower parts. The request for Mr. Zelakavic, the chief operative in the Rama Brigade, asked for help from the neighbouring brigade. We were the nearest there. I mobilised the brigade. I informed my superiors, who was Mr. Siljeg, and gave him a 24-hours' notice to move. That is, I gave 24 hours' notice to my soldiers to be ready to move. I arrived there on the night of the 24th. I entered the town, myself and a few staff members. In the town itself, it was nightfall. I saw no serious collateral damage except for one burning house in the centre of town and one body with -- in fatigues, laying in the middle of the street. However, I still heard fighting in the -- on the outskirts of the town itself, and on the hills surrounding the town. I liaisoned with the Rama Brigade commander, and it was decided, because the deteriorating situation in the vicinity and for security measures, to send in the brigade, or parts of my brigade, which arrived the next day, set up our perimeter, a security perimeter, because we then had no clear idea of troop disposition. We started to take fire from the villages of Here, Scipe and Kute. That is the first time that members of the brigade were killed, my brigade, killed and captured and wounded in the conflict, Muslim/Croat conflict. That night, I called HVO headquarters and I spoke personally to General Praljak, and my exact words to him is: "We have to stop this madness before it escalates." He informed me that "pregovori," the English translation escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objections?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- negotiations --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- between the HVO and the TO and he informed me as quickly as possible on when a decision was made. The next morning I took a column of armoured vehicles. There was a tank in the column. It was actually -- it was a small task force of company size. With me went the Rama Brigade commander. The commander at the time was Mr. Beljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And after that, did the conflict calm down? Did the delegation arrive? Did they visit Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... testimony. Had we had any intention at that time of cleansing the Muslim population, we could have clearly gone to Jablanica, at least the tunnel, the tunnel leading into Jablanica, because the "Reci" party I had sent out before, it's reconnaissance parties, notified me that there were no forces holding that route. I stopped the column at the first village south of Prozor, got out of the armoured vehicle, took a local man with me, and went to the first few villages to pacify the civilians, both Croat and Muslim, to tell them the talks were progressing, they would find a political solution to this problem. I also have to say that there's a Chinese proverb which says: Burning water won't save -- distant water won't save your burning house. Had I known that a conflict was about to ensue, had there been a joint plan of some kind to take the town of Prozor, I would have that night mobilised forces and moved them to striking distance to intervene as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did the conflict in Prozor stop? Did the delegations come? Do you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That same day, a joint delegation came up from Jablanica with representatives, both civilian and military. I recall that the army -- the Muslim general, Arif Pasalic, was there, as was Martin Zaric, the head of the HDZ in Jablanica. This ended that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us: What did you mean when you said -- when you were last time in the Tribunal? Have you already testified?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was here in February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You testified in a courtroom? Oh, you mean this statement that you gave to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. I meant -- but we know that. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We'll come to that later on. But please be so kind. My next question: You, personally, your personal knowledge, do you have any whether the HVO ever conducted any offensive actions against the TO or MOS or the BH army, whatever the name might be, that is, any components of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no indications that this actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And were you attacked by those forces? In these incidents that you spoke about, who attacked whom? Who caused the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A radicalisation of the military and civilian leadership, in joint Muslim/Croat municipalities, led to the polarisation and the conflict. The arrival of Muslims from Sandzak, Iran, Morocco and other countries, plus I would say the ethnic occupation, with some previously Croat communities, led to the destabilisation and conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: General, I will now show you two exhibits marked D174 and D175.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First D174.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please be so kind as to -- Witness, will you please be so kind as to read out this one sentence in Croatian, and the year and the month, because we have not yet translated it now.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incidence of the BH army against the HVO in 1992, from May to December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's have it on the ELMO. You have the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does this show, according to what you personally know, the incidents which caused -- which were caused by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the HVO? Were these the ones, and how did they all start, based on your personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, we object to both the relevance of this testimony and to the basis of this witness's testimony. We are again back -- this is nothing more than expert opinion. If he was in a particular action, as he did when he said it was in Prozor, and if he wants to say about what he did and what he knows of personal knowledge, certainly the Court has observed we have not objected to that. But now he's being tendered to talk about conflicts all over the map, and he's not an expert and he's is simply here expressing opinions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we will see what this witness is going to tell us and to see whether it's related to the subject-matter of this case. Mr. Krsnik, you have to bear in mind the objections raised by the Prosecutor and try to concentrate your questions which might be relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... hear what the witness has to answer the question rather than you give the answer by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honours. That is why I brought the witness. I merely wish him to give us his position from 1992 to 1993, until the 30th of June in Mostar. And we seek personal knowledge to hear only about things where the witness was personally present or his officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I think it's vital to underline, to describe the routes of the Muslim/Croat conflict, which any chronology would show, any logical chronology, the traces -- from the outset, as I described in a -- as I described, from the summer of 1992 until the signing of the Washington Agreement, would show that many of these conflicts started at the local level. They were spontaneous, and later they snowballed into a larger conflict. I believe I came to the conflict in Uskoplje, which was the first serious, I think it was a war, which ended in January of 1993. The graphics here, I don't want to describe every incident, but prior to the start of the conflict in Mostar, which I don't see clearly on the map here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You have another map, 75.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of that conflict, as I've mentioned, in Mostar, the entire municipality, Croat municipality -- the majority of Croatians were cleansed from the municipality of Konjic, by the end of -- by the start of that conflict in Mostar. Other conflicts simultaneously broke out, or in that same time frame, in Central Bosnia. People that I speak to sometimes about this fail to realise, because the majority of them were never on the terrain itself, where the fighting took place. Much of it took place in inaccessible terrain, ranging from 300 metres to 2.000 above sea level. And any cursory examination, any military historian, would understand that the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not one or two conflicts, although the Republika Srpska was the main aggressor, backed by forces from Yugoslavia. It was a series of conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some where Muslim fought Croat. In some areas there was no Muslim/Croat conflict, for example, the Posavina area, in Bihac. In Bihac, Muslim fought Muslim. In many of these separate conflicts, the common denominator was biological survival. Croatians, as the smallest minority, could not wage a war on two fronts, nor was there any tension to fight their Muslim neighbours. But as I explained before, the Muslim leadership clearly had plans, and there are documents available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I apologise for interrupting, but I must object. Now the witness says "the Muslims clearly had plans." I'd like to know the basis for his personal knowledge to assert that, what the Muslim plans were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, give us an explanation about that, whether you have personal knowledge about the existence of those plans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen document that are dated, for example, one of numerous documents that are dated in early 1993, I believe the third month, which clearly show Muslim intentions. One of those documents, signed by the SDA representative in Mostar, and now a deceased general, Arif Pasalic, spoke of forming a united Muslim front. There's one thing I would like to add, which I saw as the first indicator that dialogue between Croatians and Muslims had broken down completely. In the summer of 1992, I took my headquarters to Jablanica to start joint operations with the TO there, the Territorial Defence. They were asked to make a return visit to Tomislavgrad. They never arrived. Joint plans were also made for the liberation of Kupres. Officers from the TO in Uskoplje, General Praljak, myself, and others, were also at a meeting in Uskoplje in the summer of 1992. Nothing of this materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: These were joint operations -- Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You have mentioned that Uskoplje, there was a real war in Uskoplje, and how did that end? You wanted it tell us that.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war started in the municipality itself and escalated. Again, attempts were made to stop the fighting. I sent up my 2 IC to Bugojno. Juergen Schmidt, with another officer, and they successfully stopped, through negotiations, the conflict then from spreading north to Bugojno. With the help of BritBat, I believe the Cheshire Regiment, constant talks were -- there were ongoing talks at the local ball-bearing factory, which led to a final ceasefire agreement towards the end of January. During that conflict, my 2 IC, three other members of my staff, were captured by MOS - these MOS were from Jajce, people we had fed, clothed, armed - and they were captured and executed, with shots to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what happened with Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict in Bugojno did not escalate until November of 1993. Then the scenario was the same as in Konjic. The entire Croat population was cleansed from the Bugojno municipality. As you know, there were caps at the stadium and other places, just as they were in Jablanica museum and other areas where my brigade was stationed to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Here often the name of Mr. Zarko Tole was mentioned. Do you personally know Mr. Zarko Tole? Can you tell Their Honours where he came from, what kind of an officer, what rank and what was he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I first met Zarko Tole in Kupres at the start of the conflict in the April of 1992. I assumed that he was a member of the improvised headquarters in Grude, and I knew he was an ex-JNA officer. I know he was born in Ljute Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where is Ljute Dolac?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's the last I saw of him until after the war, because he was captured, and the details of his capture are still unclear, because before the start of the Muslim/Croat confrontations, it was rumoured that he was sold to the Republika Srpska side by Muslim extremists in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And for how long was he detained, and where?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this also because my brother was also captured, and he saw Tole, his driver Ugrin, and another man which I don't -- I know his name, but I can't remember. It escapes me at the moment. Where they were tortured, starved, and disfigured for over a year. When I saw him after the war, I had serious doubts about his mental state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we come to Mostar area in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to come close to the era of Mostar, and I wanted him -- he wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to explain all these operations which were carried out by the ABH [as interpreted], and so if he didn't have the personal knowledge, because the witness didn't -- wasn't personally there in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I wanted to ask him what was the final operation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or of the Muslim component in 1993, and why was Mostar an important strategic point for them, including Konjic and along Neretva River, and whether you personally participated in the defence.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is such that the road from Jablanica to Mostar, every square inch is almost vital for defence, basically a lifeline. And it's also an outlet to the sea. As the final operation of the MOS forces proved, at the beginning of August/end of September 1993. That operation was called Operation Neretva. I'm familiar with the terrain which surrounds Jablanica, because I held the line from Strop, which is to the right of Doljani, to Boksevica, which is on the left, which is a dominant feature that overlooks Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were there preconditions in order to ensure and implement the plan in Jablanica in 1993? What were the Muslims to hold in order to implement this plan, and what did they have to conquer? What do you personally know about the plan itself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to clear the eastern side of the Neretva River, enforce the road, communication Jablanica/Mostar, and thereby create the conditions for further progression towards the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does Sovici and Doljani have any strategic importance in this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Explain it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sovici is actually -- would be the -- is the gateway to the plateau of Risovac, which leads to all the communications that tie in western Herzegovina and the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know who held the strategic point in this area of Sovici -- of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we have a clarification of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you come to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are we still talking August/end of September 1993 now, about the Sovici answers that the witness just gave, that he could assist with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which year and at what period you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... start in September -- August/September 1993. They started earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, Sovici was held by MOS. What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning -- at the beginning of April 1993, or perhaps earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell us: Do Sovici and Doljani, do you have personal knowledge of that, since you were close to Doljani? And do they also protect the flank of Jablanica in the Neretva operation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did it represent a very important or maybe the most important strategic point for the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area of operations, Boksevica, Oklanica, or Pisvir, better known as Pisvir, which runs through Doljani, and Sovicka Vrata, which are the door that leads us, as I said, to the plateau of Risovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the last question prior to the recess: You were personally in Jablanica. What were the quantum of forces in MOS, and what is the distance between Jablanica and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a fairly accurate battle order of the MOS forces in Jablanica at the time, because I held that line from almost the end of April 1993, until the signing of the Washington Agreement. There was a local brigade called Brigada Neretvica. At times, components of the Prozor Battalion were also stationed there, as were other units, so-called "Special Units," like, for example, Crni Labudovi, Handzar Divizija, which is not actually a division, but probably a company side, also "Zuka's criminals," who were the actual force and the actual -- they decided what happened in Jablanica. There were also volunteers from Sandzak, and also Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Where is Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sandzak is the Muslim enclave within -- excuse my geography, but I believe within Serbia itself. From my experience, from talks with individuals, like Samo Siketic, the chief of staff for the MOS forces in the Bugojno area and the chief negotiator during the fighting in Uskoplje - he was also from Sandzak - and these individuals represented some of the members, apart from those from North African countries, Iran, and Pakistan, who presented the most radical wing of the MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was the force?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minimum two and a half thousand; maximum men that are armed, three and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we will have a recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume 10 minutes after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: One question for the end, and then we'll move towards your zone. Do you know what the -- personally what the fate was, namely, in the indictment, it's been asserted that HVO carried out ethnic cleansing of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Krsnik, you will find that Jablanica itself is a microcosm of the general Croatian population. At the end of the conflict, Muslim/Croat conflict, because at the beginning of the war, the Croatian population was about 18 per cent of the total population of Jablanica. And if you go to Jablanica now, you will find that there's probably 6 per cent, or less, of the Croatian population remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April, May, and June, do you know what was happening in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jablanica municipality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The fate of the Croats, what, in truth, happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993, Doljani was attacked by MOS, and 40 or 50 people were killed, half of them civilians, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe we could have a bit more specificity as to date, except for all of 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. Would you please tell us the time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which year and which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the summer of 1993, on the feast day of Ilinden -- I may need some help here, because it's the seventh month. It was the seventh month.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... attacked from three sides by MOS. The end result of that action was the death of approximately 50 people, half of them civilians. The rest were soldiers, the majority who were killed after they were captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do apologise. I don't want to try the Chamber's President, but again I must object to tu quoque nature of this. We have said from day one of this trial that bad things were done, committed by all sides. My personal sympathies, and I'm sure the Office of the Prosecutor's personal sympathies and condolences go out to all victims on all sides, but this is simply tu quoque and is not relevant to the issues before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just tell us the facts, the population ratio at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the indictment says that the HVO cleansed Jablanica, and I asked what had happened in Jablanica. That is, I am questioning the indictment. Doljani is a municipality of Jablanica. But let us move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What happened to Croats living in Jablanica? Did they cleanse anyone? What was their lot, of the Croats in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there because we liberated the area later. Approximately 220 civilians, men, women, and children, were taken to the Jablanica museum and incarcerated there, in inhuman conditions. Back to your original question: During my visit to Jablanica to start the joint Muslim actions, joint Croat actions, against Republika Srpska forces in the municipality of Konjic, there was still a semblance of cooperation between the civilian authorities, that is, Croat, Muslim civilian authorities. By the time the conflict broke out, I think I mentioned before that by the end of the third month, 1993, the majority of Croatians from Opstina Konjic - and this also includes Jablanica -- I don't wish to belabour the Tribunal here with details, but every village, the ethnic population of that village is well documented. I have given to this Tribunal. The concluding answer -- the conclusion to the answer is, is Croatians were jailed, ethnically cleansed, and removed from positions of any type of authority, not just authority, but from normal -- they were not to direct work, of course. They were marginalised. And the end result is, as I said, which is evident today, is the population has dropped from 18 per cent to 6 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about the lot of villages between Konjic and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... torched. I can only mention Trusina for one, Vrce, other villages. One look at the situation, the situation map, in the summer of 1993, of Opstina Konjic and Jablanica would show exactly how many villages were burnt, plundered, and the population run off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you still did not answer the question put by the counsel. The issue is not whether the Muslim ethnically cleansing of the Croats. The question is whether the HVO ethnically cleansed the Muslims in that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the municipality of Jablanica, in the municipalities of Jablanica, Prozor, Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... possibility. First, they had neither the weapons nor the organisation, nor the numbers to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Look at the transcript. You'll see that we've again lost something because you are just too fast, and I think that the question is missing from the transcript. And your answer, I believe, when you said that it was physically impossible to do. Will you slow down, please. Just look at the transcript. Look at the transcript. See what it looks like?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can continue with the conclusion. My answer was that the Croatians neither had the weapons, nor the organisation, nor the numbers to attempt to ethnically cleanse members of the Muslim minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Minority?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me: When did these attacks on Croat villages happen, and all that that you told us about? Which month, which year, in the municipalities of Jablanica and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The start was in the middle of, approximately, the third month of 1993. And the last Croatian was cleansed by the end of the seventh month of that same year. The last village that fell into MOS hands was Klis. I was in Boksevica when the civilian population fled, and we loaded them on trucks and turned them over to the authorities in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It is also claimed here, namely, the indictment alleges that you, the brigade, the HVO, enjoyed the support of the Croatian army from the Republic of Croatia throughout. Now you can answer.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can quote a document which I saw as an example, a document showing the battle order of HVO forces in the municipality of Uskoplje from Crni Vrh on the right, to Turajci on the left. Those are dozens and kilometres of difficult territory. This order -- actually, it's a report. It's a report of -- battle readiness report by Zeljko Siljeg, the OZ commander, and it shows that he had no more, at that critical time, the summer of 1993, than 4.000 men, approximately, to hold that difficult line, defence line. It shows every unit by name and number. A lot of those men were wounded, physically broken, and had been on the line for months, with no relief in sight. They were outnumbered in every sector. They suffered heavy casualties. Close to 500 HVO troops died in and around Uskoplje, and almost three times as many were wounded. Neither the unit indication or the number of men there indicates that the HV was present there. I will ask a rhetorical question. A war in Croatia ended, except for several operations, which lasted weeks, in January of 1992. Up to the time period which I mentioned, almost a year and a half, in which the Croatian army armed, trained, and consolidated its forces, how many reserve brigades, not professional, did they have available to send to that critical area of the front? At that time, I remind you, they had seven fully professional brigades in the HV. To continue the answer, in my sector, there were never any HV troops. The Kralj Tomislav Brigade held the line, which I mentioned already, from Strop on the right, to Kucani almost. On the left was the Jajce Brigade, or the remnants of it, and on the other side was the Domobran unit, the Doljani Battalion, Mijat Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: General, we heard here three or four representatives of the international community, European monitors, ECCM. I believe there was one representative, and Sir Martin Garrod. They did not speak much about the Mostar area, did not say they saw all that many HVs, but your area, and I say that was Uskoplje, in your area they saw HV troops. It is very difficult to believe, once you have a member of the international community in this Court and he says that before this Honourable Court. Of course, we asked what -- they said we saw vehicles with HV plates. Of course, they don't know who was in those vehicles. That a general, Andric, sir Martin who said that, some General Andric, who represented the Croatian army there. I'm telling you this in order to elicit from you what you personally know about this, or that they saw HV insignia on the plates. I do not think that they talked about troops, but that these were merely some indications?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This was a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by Mr. Krsnik and characterising the testimony of other witnesses is completely improper and I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to explain what we heard in this courtroom. I wanted to invite the witness to comment. I must say what representatives or witnesses said here in open sessions. Your Honours, I know what kind of a battle I'm waging here, and that is why I wish to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What will you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I will say, and I said earlier in yesterday's statement, that the majority of people that I saw, that may have been formerly in the HV, were people that were born in the municipalities in western Herzegovina or other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: As a commander, did you have any difficulties or did those soldiers arrive with HV patches when they came, and how did they come to say your brigade or your zone, your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my command, who were not Croatian citizens --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, excuse me. My question was: People who gave, people who gave -- I mean not leave -- [As interpreted] were they people who had come from the Croatian army and kept their Croatian army patches?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Previous translation continues] ... case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what did you do then? Did you allow it? What was done about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... voluntary basis. From my perspective as a commander, if a soldier showed up as willing to participate actively in the brigade, I accepted his participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you allow them to wear different patches on your uniforms? I'm sorry. Let me ask you first. Did the HVO have any official insignia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We finally introduced a formal rank structure, and earlier many units wore unauthorised patches on their shoulders showing their unit, which usually had the brigade emblem which ... But as for HV patches, I personally don't recall anyone in my brigade wearing HV patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It is not in the transcript again, so please look at the transcript. Which year did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... My structure and its corresponding ranks which were worn on the uniform, was not introduced, in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I've forgotten the question. Oh, yes. This is what I wanted to ask you: The Prosecutor has produced many orders and shown them to many witnesses here. Not going into whether those orders were authentic, but various witnesses testified about them, that they were orders to remove HV patches in order to disguise their affiliation. Do you know of any such orders to remove HV patches, and why would such orders be made?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my answer is I don't recall such an order, and to be truthful, the position that I was in, as a commander, that topic, to me, was not a priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, General, the next question. The Prosecutor here alleges that following the 16th of April, 1993, in different areas, that the HVO arrested and disarmed Muslims who were in the HVO only because they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to accentuate what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry. So did you have any Muslims in your brigade, in your zone?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you disarm them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the seventh month of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was such at the time, in the summer of 1993, the Muslim/Croat conflict had reached catastrophic proportions. In the unit itself I had approximately 400 to 500 soldiers of Muslim faith who were, until that date, an integral part of the brigade. I treated them no differently than any other member of that brigade. When weapons started to disappear and when refugees from other cities that had fallen poured into Tomislavgrad, there was at one point, I believe, 13.000 from Jajce alone - the security of the town itself became questionable. I wanted to avoid the same scenario that had been repeated elsewhere, and I took the decision to disarm the Muslim component.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you incarcerate them? Did you expel them? So they stayed in Tomislavgrad? And what happened in the neighbouring community, municipality, in Livno? Was there any disarmament there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my answer to your first question was no, they were not jailed, cleansed. Their property wasn't pillaged. As for Livno, a conflict broke out there the next day, the following day, and there were dead and wounded on both sides. I believe the decision I made was correct at the time, because to understand the situation then, you have to realise there was only one route in and one route out, through Central Bosnia, where conflicts were taking place, and troops returning from the front line could very easily turn on the Muslim population to create an incident. There would be retaliation and then we'd have fighting in the villages. There was one incident which was more -- nothing to do with planned ethnic cleansing, but a mindless crime, which I believe you were informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer, shortly after the disarmament, I was called by the UNPROFOR commander, Major Bauer, who was stationed in Tomislavgrad, and he mentioned to me that people had been killed in a village on the northern part of the town. I arrived there with the UNPROFOR commander and I noticed there were seven people killed. This was not done by members of the brigade but transients, who later crossed the border in one of the 350 illegal crossings, or legal crossings, and escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you personally know that these people had been apprehended and also tried?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... found out later. Yes. I found out later that there were citizens of the Republic of Croatia, and they were tried in Croatian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We are coming to the close, Mr. Glasnovic. I would like to wind up and come to the close of your testimony. Here it's also being alleged, namely, the Prosecution claims that HVO did not allow the passage of humanitarian convoys with humanitarian aid, neither of the national and international convoys. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you, as I said before, that the only road into Central Bosnia was "route triangle," that went from Tomislavgrad, through Prozor, and then Bugojno and the rest of Central Bosnia. And all classes of equipment, from food, clothing, and of course weapons, ammunitions, went along that route. This went on, from what I know, until even until 1993, and after. For example, again, at the height of the Muslim/Croat conflict, a convoy of 350 tractor and trailers used that route to go to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were the convoys examined? Did you examine these convoys and did UNPROFOR participate in weapons smuggling? And if you have any personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but again I object to relevance. My concern is also that the reason this goes on and on is that -- I don't know how long this is going to take us into tomorrow, but if we go on and on with this sort of testimony, then I will not be rushed to finish my cross-examination within some deadline set for tomorrow, if this testimony just simply goes on and on and on about, in our view, irrelevant matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Krsnik says that his direct examination will come to an end very soon. And Mr. Krsnik, we believe that your question has some relevance to the issue. The question you asked especially concerning the international organisations smuggling weapons. It's a leading question. Drop that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour, it was a lead, because, Your Honour, I've been working for 20 days every day, [As interpreted], and I apologise if some lead question comes out, but it's not intentional. It's due to fatigue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But to cut the story short, I will show you a document which was translated into English, and it bears the figure D1/331.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would kindly ask the registrar to distribute this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you read this document? Tell us the date, whether you've been acquainted with it. I see it's Tomislavgrad, and who is the gentleman who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The document speaks for itself, but tell us: Did this occur frequently?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... report. This report I'm holding is from an intelligence operative who was not directly under my command, but which I worked with, and it describes weapons parts and packing found --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Don't speak about the document. It speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Canadian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you know that personally, except for its written in here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did it happen frequently?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons, communications equipment were smuggled on a regular basis, especially after the embargo was imposed on the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But General, but this is a UN convoy.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my answer. We found weapons -- my answer is we found weapons on other convoys carrying so-called humanitarian aid, for example, bags of flour. We found communications equipment, welded into other -- into vehicle parts. As for the UN convoy, that file, that individual file, was passed on to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the convoys have free passage, unobstructed passage, or was there a permanent examination and control of that, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think it's logical when you enter or depart from a zone where there's a conflict raging, you have to be extremely careful of personnel and equipment and weapons that are entering that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then reports come in from monitors, and I'm -- the UN reports, or of the observers, that the HVO does not allow the passage of UN convoys?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer: Tomislavgrad was the centre -- central headquarters and base, the main logistics base, from where the UN forces that pushed supplies, humanitarian supplies and others, into Central Bosnia. As a matter of fact, most of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever prevent them in that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was directly responsible in negotiations with the BritBat in Tomislavgrad that gave them access to a base, base facilities, to be more exact, quarters where they held their men. The base was our logistics base, which we gave to them. The elementary school served as their quarters. From the beginning of "Operation Grapple," which was the name of the operation, to push supplies into Bosnia-Herzegovina. Every effort was made, at that end of the supply route, to help with this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the last two questions in connection with Tomislavgrad and then we'll pass on to the final questions. The witness, Allan Knudsen, at a public session testified here that he was a soldier in your ranks, that President Tudjman came to Tomislavgrad and that he lined up your men there to inspect them, and that you refused to be present because you disliked Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the name, Allan Knudsen. I can't recall at the moment because I had a platoon, reinforced platoon of over 50 internationals in my brigade. As for not liking President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The question -- first question: Was President Tudjman ever in Tomislavgrad and was there ever a line-up of your men for him? And he came to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait. We did not get an answer. I'm sorry. Witness, would you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is pure fiction. President Tudjman did come to Tomislavgrad. He was there for half an hour, there for lunch, and departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When was that? What month and what year?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is: I believe, because I can't remember the exact month, it was after the meeting between UN officials, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Tudjman, in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The next witness, it was not a public session, therefore I will describe him as Witness X, stated that he was, during his travels, arrested, incarcerated in Tomislavgrad, that he was tortured there, held captive about a month, and taken down from a bus as one of the travellers on the bus, and that in some monastery, be it of monks or nuns, but that it was a monastery in Tomislavgrad that many Muslims were also there and that they were being tortured. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11357 to 11370.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be: On whose order, what time period, what place, and all the other elements that go into writing an incident report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The question really is: Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know nothing of this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, that's what your answer should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was there any prison or camp for Muslims in Tomislavgrad? Did BritBat and the UN organisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, Tomislavgrad is not in the indictment, even on that basis, and again it's simply no more than tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the case, Your Honours. I kindly request the Prosecutor, when his witnesses -- where he said, this is very relevant, that the Court should hear that, and he invoked Article 5 of the Statute in connection with that. And now he is contradicting himself already on a number of occasions. Why did we have to listen to all of that from the Prosecutor, but we're not allowed to give the side -- to hear the defence? He, in fact, said that crimes were widespread throughout Bosnia. And when the Defence said it's not relevant to the indictment, he said something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you're allowed to ask all the questions by the Trial Chamber which we deem to be relevant, and so far the President has said they are relevant. My interjection at that stage was that it was obvious, that a simple answer was possible instead of a series of questions. Now, don't get excited. Just get on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to offer you the entire truth, and that is why I've invited -- I'm bringing in all these witnesses. This Court must know what the truth is, to hear what happened in Tomislavgrad. I don't have any other witness from Tomislavgrad, and there's nobody else from -- that was my idea, to give a picture. The idea was to refute the indictment, the items, and to challenge it, and to have you hear the truth of the events there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, all we're saying is there's a way to do it. You've asked this witness whether he was aware that such a -- whether he was aware of the incident. He was unaware. The next obvious question is: Do you know of any monastery or nunnery that was used as a Detention Centre for Muslims. And if he says no, well then we move on to the rest of it. But you haven't posed that question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've asked. I've asked whether prisons or camps existed. Then the Prosecutor interjected. And the witness said -- answered no. And I've ended -- I will end with that, and we come to the concluding questions. But let me ask once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, was there a prison or a camp for Muslims in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to the final question. Witness, do you remember when you talked to me for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was in the winter of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you remember when we met the next time, the second time after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you, on both occasions, give your approval to testify on behalf of the Defence? Did you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when I was here for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we missed the answer again, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: During our first meeting, did you accept to be the Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not said the answer. Witness, wait at least for 30 seconds after the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer to the question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we've lost everything. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you, during the first meeting we had, did you accept to become a Defence witness for this trial, during our first meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did we have, the two of us, any contact from that moment up to February 2002?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did I then establish contact with you in February, did I ask you then to meet with you again? Did I invite you then to come and testify?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did you give any other statement to somebody else meanwhile, and if yes, to whom, and when? In this Tribunal, I mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who was it that you gave a statement to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the Tribunal

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we're curious. Why would somebody who makes a decision to be a Defence witness in the year 2000, then offer himself as a Prosecution witness in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Because of that I ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're interested to hear the answer. And what value would he be to the Prosecution? Why do we need to know this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was. You'll hear it all. Don't let me answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Tribunal or the Prosecutor? Do you know who you gave the statement to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. Wait, wait, wait. We still have not catch up the answer. You answered too fast, Witness. The question is: Did you give a statement to the Tribunal or the Prosecutor? Do you know who you gave the statement to? You may answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the 13 investigating teams that are organic to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what happened? Where did you get this statement? Where did you go? Did you give a statement? What happened? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was contacted in January -- 12th month of 2001, by a member of the team, and they asked me to speak to them in Sarajevo. At the time, I was assistant to the Minister of Defence for military matters, and I answered to them that if the minister approved my meeting the team, that I would do so. They sent a letter to the minister approving my interview with them. He approved the request. We had one preliminary meeting in Sarajevo, and they asked me where I wished to hold the interview. I told them it didn't matter to me, and they suggested that I come to The Hague, since it was cheaper, me coming here, than the whole team going there, to Sarajevo, that is. The exact date escapes me, but I remained here for three days, answered questions, flew back to Sarajevo and waited for the final rendition of my witness statement. I was presented with a witness statement, I read the witness statement, and I immediately contacted two individuals within the Ministry of Defence to serve as witnesses to verify that I would not sign the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I gave you the letter later. I can, not verbatim, but I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you would be so kind this is the proof, Exhibit 330. No B/C/S. Just English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you give us the reasons why you refused to sign it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the witness statement was totally subjective. The majority of what I had said was left out, what I thought was important. And actually, I was a bit disappointed, because I assumed that a witness should be someone who tries to tell the objective truth and not a useful idiot. If you wish, I can read the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, no. We have it. Tell us: Were you threatened during the interview, that you would be sent to gaol, for instance, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is: I worked in a correctional system for almost a decade, and there was a small -- there was an attempt to play the "Mutt and Jeff" routine with me, but I more or less shrugged it off and spoke what I assumed to be the truth. That's why I gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was it perhaps taped?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told that the interview would not be taped, and when I read the witness statement, I asked myself: What does "substantially verbatim" mean in the introductory page to my statement? My conclusion is that a witness statement should be just that, a statement, given by the witness, and not a creative writing project, which terms like "style" -- term like "style" were mentioned in the writing of this statement. I don't know what style has to do with giving evidence. Therefore, I was more disenchanted than frustrated, actually. The first thing I asked the interviewers is: "What took you so long?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So long for what?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had a proper -- I think I had a front-row seat to the events that transpired in the former Yugoslavia. By that I mean there were theatres of operation, zones of interest where I was engaged --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did I get you right? When I asked you why did it take them so long, did you mean why did they wait so long to contact you and invite you to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, that was it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And did you say the same thing or things that you said before the Court? Did you provide them with some documentation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I basically stated the same things that I'm stating now. I gave numerous documents and other pieces of evidence which I considered crucial to my -- to back my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did anyone ask you - and if yes, then yes; if not, then not - whether you would be coming to testify here in The Hague? You did not tell them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you volunteer that information? Because, after all, you couldn't be a witness on two sides, could you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm asking you to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So are you saying that you told someone that you had already agreed to give evidence for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, what did you understand by my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my -- let me explain the background to this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: No. I asked you a very simple question. I asked you whether, when you were being interviewed, you told the interviewers that you had already decided to give evidence for the Defence. Because, as an army man, and somebody who has worked in a correctional institution, you know you can't give evidence on two sides. So did you tell them that you had already met with the Defence and that you were giving evidence for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was approached for the last -- since 1996 to be called as a witness, a potential witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. That's not an answer. Why didn't you tell them? Because your first question was: What took you so long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought I had something to say as far as the criminal acts committed in my zone of operations, and I would have gladly given my statement had they asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Colonel, or General, you're used to dealing with subordinate officers. I'm asking you a very simple question. Why did you not deem it appropriate to tell the Prosecution, first off: I have already agreed to give evidence as a witness for the Defence? Because you know you cannot give evidence on two sides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I at the time assumed I would never be called as a witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, did you tell Mr. Krsnik, you know, there may be problems about my giving evidence for you because I might be a Prosecution witness? Did you think to tell Mr. Krsnik that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only spoke once, and I spoke through an intermediary, to be a witness for the Defence. I didn't meet Mr. Krsnik or talk with him at any length or ask for legal advice until after the witness statement I gave here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I add something else, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Feel free.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He called me -- notice to witness here was on very short notice, I believe several days, I think, several days before I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is indeed how it was, because when I was told that he had refused to sign the statement, I decided to take it as if he had not ever given the statement. And I'm not ashamed of that. I am glad. Perhaps that is the difference between our legal systems. I have nothing against witnesses giving their statements to Prosecutions, even as far back as seven years ago. If everybody behaved that way, perhaps everything would look differently. So this was not objection. I merely wanted to show how certain things were happening here. I have nothing against that. And I tell every witness of mine: Well, if the Prosecutor approaches you, feel free to give any statement you like. I rejoice at that. And I have to tell you that we shall have more witnesses like that, when you will see that the Prosecutor treated them with regard to Muslim witnesses 1 to 100. Thank you, Your Honours. I do not have any further questions and I apologise if I took too long. But you see, I can never envisage what will happen, either problems with interpretation or -- and every witness is a problem unto himself. I can hardly wait for the break to get some rest, and I am now being very honest with you. Thank you very much from the bottom of my heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have to have a break now. We'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Kenneth Scott. I represent the Prosecutor in this case. And in light of some of the testimony you've given, perhaps I should point out: It's correct, is it not, sir, that you and I have not met until you came and began testifying yesterday? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that you served in the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry from 1975 to 1979, and you left the service at that time with the rank of corporal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
