utterances.text: No, I did not. I served from 1975 to 1979. After leaving, I joined the Royal Edmonton Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me if I -- you were in active service from 1975 for 1979, and left with the rank of corporal; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And from 1979 to 1989, you were again a corporal in the reserve forces attached to the Royal Edmonton Regiment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Please tell me in what way it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the RER briefly in, I believe, 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long did you serve in it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for approximately a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then is this when you were a correctional officer, as you've told us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked with Alberta Corrections, which is part of the Alberta provincial government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1980 to about 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have any rank or position during that employment?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started out as a CO 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What does that mean in layman's terms?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correctional officer 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a CO 2. And then I served as the tactical team commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for how long were you in that position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two years, or probably even longer. I believe from 1985 until about 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then when did you do your service in the French Foreign Legion? I would suggest some years, but so far you've been correcting me, so I'll just ask you to clarify it, please. What years were you in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left for Europe in 1989. I joined the legion at the beginning of 1990. And when the war broke out, I returned to Croatia in August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what rank or position did you hold in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legionnaire premier class.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you can compare this to the Canadian army or if you're more familiar with it, perhaps the US military. What rank would legionnaire first class compare to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a legionnaire, you have first-class legionnaire and you have deuxieme class.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct to say that it's like a private first class in the British -- excuse me - the Canadian or American army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. My answer is: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So before you returned to Croatia, following your service with the French Foreign Legion, the highest military rank you had ever held was corporal; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, it's true, is it not, that you left the French Foreign Legion before you completed your obligation of service, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you leave at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the war had broken -- we returned from the Gulf, and we saw Yugoslavian tanks burning in Slovenia, and myself and other individuals of Croatian background decided to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were there other, as you just said, persons of Croatian background in your particular unit or close by you in the French Foreign Legion who left and went to Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a large number of Croatian nationals in the Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll answer my question. Were there people close to you or in your unit that left and went to Croatia at the same time or about the same time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several individuals that I knew, and I met more later in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who were the ones who you knew that left about the same time you did?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the 2 IC of the Zrinski Battalion in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've used that military jargon before, and I don't know that it's ever been clarified. I assume when you say "2 IC," you mean second in command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the name of this individual?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aldo Lucev.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Anyone else with you at that time to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Michael Surevic and other individuals that were in my unit, or who I met later, had served in the Legion. For example, General of the HV, Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you serve are Ante Roso, who later became the senior commander officer after Praljak of the HVO? Did you serve with Roso in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a different regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know him when you were in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was his rank in the French Foreign Legion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was a senior non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately at what time did he leave -- not a day, sir, but approximate month or time of year and the year that he left the French Foreign Legion to join the forces in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I believe he arrived in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it correct, sir, would it be correct, then, that General Roso went from being a non-commission the officer in the French Foreign Legion in 1990, to become the most senior officer over all the HVO military by approximately October/November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to ask for the floor as little as possible, but I'd like to know the relevance of this question. Is it the credibility or what is it? Why are all these questions relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the person doing the cross-examination is entitled to ask about the background of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I fail to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question, and if he has no knowledge of that, he may refuse to answer it. It's up to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me rephrase the question and ask it this way: You continued to be an active HVO by the late fall of 1993? That's clearly been your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained an active HVO member until I resigned in the fourth month of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was a simple yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just question the date, why late fall of 1993. I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, and isn't it true, and didn't you know, that the senior HVO officer, the person who took over from Slobodan Praljak, in approximately the end of November 1993, was Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what is the value of leadership in a military unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, leadership at every level is the most important component of a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to my original statement in the beginning of yesterday, to me, with my humble military background, I think it would be fair to say, from my observations, that a military unit or an organisation again is one where leadership and initiative, and therefore command and control, are present at the lowest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How would you define the most important characteristics of leadership?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience on different continents, different types of leadership styles. Not one is the same as the other. There is lead -- there is a style called "say as I do," and a style called "do as I say." In other words, there are officers, who I've met personally, who ascribe to that law that there's nothing impossible as long as you yourself don't have to do it. I think I can sum it up in one phrase, is lead by example is basically the ... And that hasn't changed since time of Gideon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you would say, sir, that the example that a leader sets for his troops in a military sense, the soldiers around him, is a very important aspect of leadership?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that would apply, sir, would it not, to both, if we can say, positive aspects of behaviour and also negative aspects of behaviour, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Leadership can be abused or misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that leadership had something to do with, your words, command and control. What is the connection between leadership in a military sense and command and control?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary difference between Eastern and Western styles, for military doctrines, is that the Western style provides a professional, a non-commissioned officer corps, which ensures leadership at those levels where the battle is fought, and that is below battalion level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not -- I'm going to try not to interrupt you any more than necessary, but because we want to cover some ground tonight, my question to you is this --. INTERPRETER: [Interpretation] Your microphone, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is the connection, please - I'm not asking for different styles between East and West - what is the connection between leadership and command and control?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two elements are interrelated, and one influences the other. A good leader makes an effort to train his men, he cares for their well-being, and I'm not too sure exactly what else I can add.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, in your business, in the military business that you've now been engaged in for some years, do you -- when you look at other officers around you, do you consider someone to be a good officer, professional officer, who does not have command and control of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question, I think you have in armies that are professional armies, that have a tradition of several centuries long, that have a military justice system --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off. In the Canadian army, in the French Foreign Legion, in the Republic of Croatia army, and in the HVO, you saw other officers around you, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't have a very high opinion of higher ex-JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you saw some officers you considered to be good officers and some people, I assume - correct me if I'm wrong - and some officers who, in your assessment, were not very good officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And coming back to my earlier question, sir, isn't part of that assessment in whether someone is a good officer or a bad officer or, for that matter, a good leader or a bad leader, is that they exercise command and control effectively over those subordinate to them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, in theory, in a military organisation that supplies all the requirements for a well-organised and disciplined force, which also means trained, this naturally is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it not often the case, in your military experience, that with special or elite units, the personal role or figure of the commander or leader is even more important?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, leadership is the most vital component of battle readiness, but I'm not too sure if I understand in what sense you mean the role of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for instance, sir, isn't it often the case that such a unit, a special unit or an elite unit, derives in some measure its identity or even its name from the leader of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that question is for -- there are regiments in the British army that have the name of monarchs, kings --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about current leaders. I'm not talking about a deceased monarch. I'm talking about the current leader. Let me give you some examples from the most relevant conflict and that's the one in Yugoslavia at the time. Did you ever know of a leader, commander, called Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it not true that his unit was often known as Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it not true, sir, that his unit, his units, were often referred to as "Arkanovci"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was fervently objected to by the Prosecutor that I was inviting speculations and some hearsay knowledge, and now the witness is being examined about Arkan or "Arkan's boys" without any knowledge, without the witness having any personal knowledge about that. So what is the foundation for these questions. The witness can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. The witness said that that's correct. It's a definite answer. He knows about that. We have to wait until the following questions that will be put forward by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And I have to say that we're having a very effective and interesting cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me cite you another example. Are you aware of another Serb commander name - and forgive me if I mispronounce it, please - Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vojislav Seselj, the ... yes, the Serb, I presume, extremist, from --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me, sir. He had a unit that was often called the "White Eagles"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't believe that was his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you don't remember that name, sir. Do you remember that his again, his soldiers, were often called "Seseljvici" [phoen], or forgive me if I --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Seseljovci."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Thank you. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I believe again -- since they were not in my zone of operations, I don't know they were one and the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember a Serb -- a group of Serb forces who were known -- commonly referred to as the "Seseljovci", or the name you just said? And again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of that group. If I could add also: There are other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Walter's Guard." There were other paramilitary units in Bosnia-Herzegovina who used animal names or other names from their mythology. For example, the Black Swans, "Sejtani". As I mentioned before, Handzar Divizija, and other units which I can name, but I think it's counterproductive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there were a number of units throughout the theatre of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia where the unit and the soldiers were closely identified by the name of the commanding officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think a systematic -- the word I'm looking for escapes me at the moment. I think a systematic examination of the units and the order of battle of the warring parties would confirm a positive -- or a negative answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question to you. You can -- I suggest you to you, you've been here and you've told us, you've claimed extensive knowledge of the war. You know it to be true, don't you, that many units, on all sides - Serb, Croat, Muslim - are identified by the name of their commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will give you the name of the four HVO guards brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. I'll move on. What you described in your testimony as "Serbinisation," that happened to both the Croats and the Muslims, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall using the term, and you were describing something in responses to questions by counsel, "Serbinisation"? If I misheard you, I apologise, but I believe you used either that term or one very similar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, he was talking about the JNA, and it might be fair to say Serbinisation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the Serbinisation of the JNA, whereby the outbreak of hostilities, the majority of the officers, which is over 80 per cent, and weapons and equipment were practically in Serbian hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my only point, sir, is: It's true, isn't it, that that phenomenon applied both equally to the Croats and the Muslim? They were both at a disadvantage because of the Serb domination of the JNA, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most definitely, except the Muslims were in a worse position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, indeed, what you've told us about the lack of military training, the lack of military organisation, that all applied at least as much to the Muslim or Bosniak side, as it did to the Croats, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that question -- not I think, but the question, it's a factual statement, is the majority of the present-day Muslim component of the Federation army and also the MOS component during the Croat/Muslim conflict was composed of ex-JNA officers. And not just ex-JNA officers, but people who were closely tied to the former apparatus in the former Yugoslavia, and by that I mean, KOS, the military counter-intelligence service, and the internal security organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is a simple one: Those facts, those circumstances, applied equally, at least equally, to both the Muslims and the Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, I, in the earlier answer, I said that the Muslims were in a worse position when war broke out in April of 1992, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is because they made no attempts, or there was very little effort made, to prepare for the oncoming aggression. If I may give you one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir. I think that's sufficient. I'll have a second question for you. Based on what you say, isn't it true, sir, that of the three ethnic groups - the Serbs, Croat, and Muslims - the Muslims were the least militarily prepared for the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, it depends on what year you're making your -- basing your statement on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've just said the beginning of the conflict, and that's what I'm talking about, at the beginning of the conflict, or as the conflict, in your view, was imminent, of the three ethnic groups, the Muslims were the least prepared; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness wanted to explain why it was so. I think it would be fair and just to allow him to explain why they were the least prepared. I think it's not an irrelevant question, that he should be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness should be allowed to explain why. He hasn't finished yet. We only heard the witness tell us: "At the beginning of the conflict."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Slovenians managed to -- managed to capture, I think, almost 30 per cent of the weapons from the former TO, Territorial Defence. As one of the former Yugoslav republics, they captured the most weapons and were able to defend themselves. In Croatia, large stockpiles were also captured by the Croatian army that also belonged to the Territorial Defence forces. Since the force structure of the former JNA was partially based on the territorial principle, this means these weapons were stored in the municipalities of the republics, where they were to be used. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the central government, which -- who Mr. Izetbegovic represented, took no steps to retain those weapons, despite the clear signal that had been sent from Croatia and Slovenia. As a result, by the end of March 1992, the Serbs -- actually, what was to be the Republika Srpska had handed out 100.000 rifles to Serbian volunteers and Serbian members of the SDS. All heavy weapons were taken from municipal stores in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the -- in 1990, after the first round of elections in the country, or republic. So I have my own personal views, and I think that Mr. Izetbegovic did not heed the lessons of the past. Unfortunately, neither did the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Witness, I have to cut you off. We are not going to hear your personal views. We want to hear the factual issues. Mr. Scott, you may continue with your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just finish that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've gone on for four minutes now on an answer which is non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, we understand what you are going to tell us. Let the Prosecutor ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you consider yourself a good officer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think an appropriate question ... my answer would be subjective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm putting the question to you in a courtroom. You're under oath. No one is going to complain if you're a bit immodest, if you wish. Just answer my question, please. Do you consider yourself a good officer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did the best I could in a difficult situation, but I think the men I served with and fought with could better answer that question, not only the men I fought with, but the members of UNPROFOR, IFOR, SFOR and RRF, the Rapid Reaction Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have command and control of your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the circumstances, it would be more a positive answer than a negative answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, can we understand that, sir, to mean that you had more command and control over your soldiers than you did not? It was more the case that you had command and control than that you didn't?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had complete command and control to that level that I would have wanted to see in my units, even after the formation of the professional brigades, because, as I said in the outset of my statement, the conditions at the time were not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, in terms of the conditions and the time, would you agree with me, sir, that leadership, the way we've talked about it this evening, leadership does not always depend on a formal position on an organisational chart, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you, because in any organisation, even this courtroom, I presume, exists a formal authority and a real authority, in other words, respect between the people that work here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And real leadership does not often count or depend upon an official appointment or a piece of paper, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a difficult question for me to answer. It's not in itself difficult, but I think any organisation, whether it's the army or a company, for that matter, needs a formal chain of command in the doctrinal -- in doctrinal knowledge that's present at all levels of command. And I don't know if that answered your question or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you: In your experience, you've known individuals, haven't you, that exercised tremendous leadership with very little formal authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that had authority, again from my experience, and I don't think I'm generalising, are people who fought the battle at the tactical levels. And 90 per cent of the war in the former Yugoslavia was fought at the tactical level. So tactical leaders were respected, because they led by example. In my brigade, for example, there was no battalion commander, or even in the brigade staff, there were few people that weren't wounded, some more than once. In my brigade headquarters, I had six people killed and eight wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again I'm going to suggest you're getting a bit far afield. My question to you, and I'll move on. This will be the last -- in your experience, sir, you've known people in formal positions who in fact were very poor leaders, and you've known other people who had very little formal authority but in fact were very effective leaders; now, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained to you, in, sir, that people that led in battle usually had authority over their men and were respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the conditions that you've described to this Chamber, in a situation involving a lack of training and a lack of discipline, is it not all the more dangerous to put such forces into a volatile situation and, if I can put it this way, light a match?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict in the former Yugoslavia was inevitable. It basically snowballed, and for every action there was a reaction. So I think your question is -- I don't fully understand the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you set such forces, such ill-trained and ill-disciplined forces in motion, there is a greater danger of things getting out of hand; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many numerous times during the war -- again, I don't want to get into my own personal experience here - I didn't really expect to see the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question. With all due respect to your military experience --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm coming --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, please come to it quickly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm coming to what I'm trying to say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When your village, when your village, your family, your home, friends are endangered, when biological survival is at stake, you don't think -- you don't ask questions; you take the best steps you can to defend yourself and your community. It's basically a "fight-or-flight" syndrome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question. Let me put it to you this way: I submit to you, sir, and indeed we all know now you did talk to the Office of the Prosecutor, is it not true, sir, that you take great pride in the fact that you exercised, in your view, quite good command and control over your soldiers; contributing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take a certain amount of pride, yes; naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So even in these difficult situations, sir, you made an effort to exercise command and control and you feel you did it more or less successfully; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can only say that that would be left up to a military analyst or a military historian to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, again I'm going to suggest to you you're being a bit too modest, and contrary to what you've said today, what you've told us before is you were basically pretty successful at exercising command of your forces. Now, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the results speak for themselves. I formed two brigades and led thousands of men, especially in the last six months of the war, and I think I did so successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to change gears a bit. That might be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this case, we'll have the break. Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Nothing. [Interpretation] I merely wished to inform the Chamber that perhaps my client is not feeling well, so perhaps he will not be coming tomorrow, and he will sign it of his own will, if he doesn't feel better, because today he is not feeling all that great, but he doesn't want me to tell you about this. But nevertheless, perhaps he will not be attending tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I have to make sure whether your client agrees that we'll continue the proceedings even without his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I just wanted to inform about this, that he will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic has indicated that maybe you haven't asked him yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, be that as it may, he does not come, we shall be able to continue with the proceedings. That is all I wished to say, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Seric. No. Yes. We'll resume tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of May 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
